case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Confrontation Clause permits a child-sex-abuse complainant to testify behind a screen blocking face-to-face confrontation with the defendant without the trial court making a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child needed that protection to avoid trauma.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause) (as applied to a courtroom screen procedure that blocks the witness’s view of the defendant).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pitts argues the trial court employed a screen that prevented his four-year-old daughter from seeing him during her testimony without making the individualized, case-specific finding of necessity that Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig require. He contends Mississippi effectively treated the screen as mandatory under a statute using 'shall,' substituting a legislatively presumed risk of trauma for the constitutionally required evidentiary showing about this particular child. He further emphasizes the record contains no actual findings (and little to no evidence) that the child would be traumatized by seeing him—indeed, the child expressed affection and a desire to hug him—so the procedure violated confrontation, and the state court’s harmless-error/alternative-evidence discussion cannot cure the structural constitutional failure to follow Coy/Craig’s prerequisites.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Mississippi argues confrontation’s 'essential elements' were satisfied because the child testified under oath (or equivalent), was subject to cross-examination, and was observable by the jury, while the screen was a permissible protective measure within the trial court’s authority. The State contends the trial court determined the screen was necessary to protect the child from trauma and that, in any event, any error was harmless because guilt was overwhelmingly proven by independent evidence, including multiple witnesses’ accounts of the child’s statements to adults/authorities and the child’s videotaped forensic interview (which the defense itself introduced). The State also resists further review because the case is fact-bound and does not warrant Supreme Court intervention.

John Roberts.reasoning: The opposing-side’s best point—pressed by Justice Alito—that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the “core” confrontation values is substantial, but Craig makes those safeguards necessary, not sufficient, when the State dispenses with face-to-face confrontation. As Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, Coy treats a screen that blocks the witness’s view of the accused as a straightforward denial of face-to-face confrontation, triggering Craig’s narrow exception—and that exception turns on a case-specific, evidence-based judicial finding of necessity that a categorical statutory “shall” cannot supply. A narrow disposition enforcing Craig’s individualized-findings prerequisite (and remanding for any harmless-error analysis as appropriate) best respects precedent and avoids converting Craig’s exception into a routine practice. No colleague identified a precedent that would permit us to relax Craig’s predicate without effectively overruling Coy/Craig, which I am not prepared to do.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The opposing-side’s strongest point—pressed most clearly in Justice Alito’s pragmatic framing—is that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the “core” confrontation values, making the screen a modest accommodation. But under the Sixth Amendment’s original public meaning, as reflected in Coy v. Iowa, the ordinary constitutional rule is face-to-face confrontation, and Maryland v. Craig permits departure only upon a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular witness needs protection from trauma caused by the defendant’s presence. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, Mississippi’s categorical “shall” cannot substitute for that constitutionally required judicial predicate, and treating it as sufficient would convert Craig’s narrow exception into a routine legislative carve-out. Any argument that the evidence was otherwise strong goes, at most, to harmless-error remedial questions on remand, not to whether the Constitution allowed dispensing with face-to-face confrontation in the first place.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is that the screen was a limited accommodation that preserved oath, cross-examination, and the jury’s ability to assess demeanor—so, functionally, confrontation was largely intact. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Coy treats a screen blocking the witness’s view of the accused as a direct denial of face-to-face confrontation, and Maryland v. Craig permits that denial only after an on-the-record, case-specific necessity finding; a statute’s categorical “shall” cannot do that constitutional work. Even on my more pragmatic, consequence-aware approach, insisting on Craig’s prerequisite is the narrower, administrable rule that prevents this exceptional measure from becoming routine without judicial scrutiny. Any argument that the evidence was strong goes, at most, to harmless error on remand, not to whether the Constitution allowed dispensing with face-to-face confrontation in the first place.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the “core” of confrontation—does not answer Coy’s premise that a screen blocking the witness’s view of the accused is a direct denial of face-to-face confrontation unless Craig’s strict predicate is satisfied. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Craig makes the accommodation conditional on an on-the-record, case-specific necessity finding tied to this particular child and to trauma caused by the defendant’s presence, not a generalized legislative judgment or an implicit acceptance by the trial court. From my pragmatic, fairness-focused perspective, allowing Mississippi’s seemingly mandatory “shall” practice to operate categorically risks routine erosion of confrontation in the very cases where reliability and power imbalances are most acute. Harmless-error arguments may bear on remedy, but they cannot retroactively supply the missing constitutional justification for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation in the first place.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s pragmatic point—that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the “core” of confrontation—has force as a policy matter, but our doctrine makes those features necessary, not sufficient, when face-to-face confrontation is denied. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Coy treats a screen blocking the witness’s view of the accused as a direct infringement, and Craig permits it only upon a case-specific, evidence-based necessity finding tied to this particular child and this defendant’s presence. Letting Mississippi’s statutory “shall” (or a trial judge’s unparticularized acceptance) do that work would convert Craig’s narrow exception into a categorical rule, undermining statutory and constitutional coherence. I therefore remain with Petitioner, with remedy/harmless-error questions appropriately left for remand as Roberts suggests.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The opposing argument—pressed most forcefully in Justice Alito’s earlier framing—that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the ‘core’ of confrontation cannot carry the day because Coy makes a screen that blocks the witness’s view of the accused a direct denial of the Sixth Amendment’s face-to-face guarantee absent a constitutionally adequate justification. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, Maryland v. Craig supplies that narrow justification only upon an evidence-based, case-specific judicial finding of necessity; a statute’s categorical ‘shall’ procedure or a trial court’s generalized concern cannot substitute for that predicate without converting Craig’s exception into a broad rule. Harmless-error or weight-of-evidence arguments may bear on remedy, but they cannot retroactively create the missing necessity finding without collapsing a textual command into a freestanding balancing test. I therefore remain with petitioner for a narrow disposition enforcing Craig’s individualized-findings requirement and remanding for further proceedings.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest opposing point (echoed by Justice Alito) is that oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved the confrontation “core,” making the screen a modest accommodation. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Coy treats a screen blocking the witness’s view of the defendant as an obvious denial of face-to-face confrontation, and Craig permits that only upon an on-the-record, case-specific necessity finding tied to this particular child and to trauma caused by the defendant’s presence. A statutory “shall” regime or an unelaborated trial-court acceptance cannot substitute for Craig’s individualized predicate without turning a narrow exception into a routine practice, which would erode administrable rules and the Court’s legitimacy. Any argument about overwhelming evidence goes to harmless-error analysis on remand, not to whether the Constitution allowed dispensing with face-to-face confrontation in the first place.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest opposing consideration is that the screen preserved oath, cross-examination, and jury observation while advancing the compelling policy of protecting child witnesses. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Maryland v. Craig makes those safeguards necessary, not sufficient: the Constitution permits dispensing with face-to-face confrontation only after a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child would suffer trauma from the defendant’s presence, and a statute’s categorical “shall” cannot supply that predicate. Justice Thomas’s original-public-meaning point reinforces that Coy v. Iowa treats a screen blocking the witness’s view of the accused as the paradigmatic confrontation denial absent such individualized necessity. Any argument that the evidence was overwhelming goes, at most, to harmless error on remand and cannot retroactively cure the missing Craig finding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument—pressed by Justice Alito—is that the screen preserved oath, cross-examination, and jury observation, and served the compelling interest of protecting child witnesses from trauma. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, Craig makes those safeguards necessary but not sufficient: the constitutional permission to depart from face-to-face confrontation turns on a case-specific, evidence-based necessity finding about this particular child, and a statutory “shall” procedure cannot substitute for that judicial predicate. Under Coy, a screen that blocks the witness’s view of the accused is the paradigmatic face-to-face deprivation, so treating individualized findings as optional would convert Craig’s narrow exception into a routine practice and erode procedural fairness in precisely the cases where accuracy is most fragile. Harmlessness or evidentiary strength cannot retroactively supply the missing constitutional determination at the moment the right was denied; at most it bears on remedy on remand.

John Roberts.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa held that using a screen to prevent the witness from seeing the defendant is a paradigmatic violation of the Sixth Amendment’s face-to-face confrontation requirement, and Maryland v. Craig permits departure from that requirement only upon a case-specific, evidence-based finding that the particular child witness needs protection to avoid trauma. Here, the procedure appears to have been applied as effectively mandatory under a statute using “shall,” without the individualized necessity findings Craig demands, which risks substituting a legislative presumption for a constitutional prerequisite. A narrow disposition restoring Craig’s requirement of individualized findings for any courtroom measure that blocks face-to-face confrontation best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy, leaving harmless-error questions for the state courts on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s text guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” which at the founding was understood to require face-to-face confrontation in open court absent a demonstrated, case-specific necessity. Coy v. Iowa holds that using a screen to block the witness’s view of the defendant violates that ordinary requirement unless the trial court makes an individualized finding of necessity, and Maryland v. Craig permits departures from face-to-face confrontation only upon an evidence-based determination that the particular child would suffer trauma from the defendant’s presence. Mississippi’s statute, Miss. Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), employs mandatory language (“shall”) and does not itself demand such case-specific findings; if the trial court likewise failed to make them, the procedure conflicts with the Confrontation Clause as construed in Coy/Craig. Whatever the strength of other evidence, the Constitution does not allow dispensing with confrontation’s face-to-face component by legislative presumption rather than judicial findings tied to this witness.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Although Coy v. Iowa recognized a strong preference for face-to-face confrontation, Maryland v. Craig permits departures where an important public policy is served and the procedure otherwise preserves the core of confrontation through oath, cross-examination, and observation by the trier of fact. Here the child testified in court, was subject to cross-examination, and was observable to the jury; the screen functioned as a narrow, practical protective measure in a child-sex-abuse case, where preventing trauma is a weighty interest. Given the trial court’s apparent acceptance of the need for protection and the substantial independent evidence the State identifies, I would not extend Coy/Craig into a rigid requirement that the record contain extensive, formalized findings before any modest shielding measure may be used. On this record, the Confrontation Clause’s essential protections were satisfied, and any deficiency in explicit, case-specific findings does not warrant reversal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa treats an in-court screen that blocks the witness’s view of the defendant as a direct denial of face-to-face confrontation, and Maryland v. Craig permits such a denial only after a case-specific, evidence-based finding of necessity that this particular child would suffer trauma from seeing the defendant while testifying. Here, Mississippi’s use of a mandatory “shall” screen procedure without individualized findings substitutes a legislative presumption for the Sixth Amendment requirement and risks becoming routine—precisely what Coy and Craig forbid. Protecting child victims is a compelling interest, but it must be pursued through constitutional means; trial courts retain broad remedial tools (e.g., support persons, courtroom management) yet must make the Craig necessity finding before denying face-to-face confrontation. Because the constitutional prerequisite was not satisfied, the Confrontation Clause was violated notwithstanding other evidence of guilt.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa recognizes a Sixth Amendment preference for face-to-face confrontation, permitting departures only when “necessary to further an important public policy,” and Maryland v. Craig allows child-witness shielding procedures only upon a case-specific, evidence-based finding of necessity that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence. A screen that blocks the witness’s view of the defendant is a direct restriction on face-to-face confrontation, so a statutory “shall” or generalized legislative judgment about child trauma cannot substitute for Craig’s individualized judicial finding. Because the record here lacks an adequate, particularized necessity finding tied to this child, the procedure fails Craig’s prerequisite and thus violates the Confrontation Clause even if other “elements” (oath, cross-examination, jury observation) were otherwise present. Workability and coherence favor a clear rule: trial courts may use screens for child witnesses only after making explicit, individualized necessity findings on the record as Craig requires.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s Confrontation Clause guarantees the accused a face-to-face meeting with the witnesses against him, and this Court has held that any departure from that rule demands an individualized, case-specific finding of necessity. Coy v. Iowa makes clear that a screen deliberately preventing a witness from seeing the defendant triggers the face-to-face requirement, and Maryland v. Craig permits dispensing with it only upon “a proper finding of necessity” grounded in evidence that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence. A legislature’s categorical “shall” procedure (or a trial court’s unparticularized invocation of child protection) cannot substitute for the constitutionally required finding, and without it the screen procedure violates the Confrontation Clause notwithstanding arguments about overwhelming evidence or harmlessness.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa held that a screen blocking face-to-face confrontation is an “obvious” Confrontation Clause violation absent a constitutionally sufficient justification, and Maryland v. Craig permits dispensing with face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific, evidence-based finding that this particular child needs protection to avoid trauma. Here, the use of a mandatory-like “shall” screen procedure without individualized findings appears to substitute a legislative presumption for the trial court’s duty under Craig to “hear evidence and determine” necessity, which is inconsistent with the Sixth Amendment as applied through Coy/Craig. While Craig recognizes protective measures that preserve oath, cross-examination, and observation, that permission is conditioned on the requisite necessity finding, and the absence of that predicate makes the procedure unlawful regardless of the State’s post hoc harmlessness arguments. Respect for precedent and administrable rules counsels enforcing Coy/Craig’s clear prerequisite rather than allowing a categorical screen without record-supported findings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s text guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and this Court has read that to include a literal face-to-face encounter absent a justified exception. Coy v. Iowa held that a physical screen preventing the witness from seeing the defendant is an “obvious” confrontation violation unless the denial of face-to-face confrontation is justified, and Maryland v. Craig permits such a deviation only after a case-specific, evidence-based finding that the particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence (not merely by the courtroom generally). If the trial court employed a screen based on a categorical statutory preference (“shall”) without individualized findings supported by evidence about this child, it failed to satisfy Craig’s prerequisite for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation. Precedent therefore compels holding that the screen procedure was unconstitutional on this record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment’s Confrontation Clause protects face-to-face confrontation as a core component of a fair adversarial process, and Coy v. Iowa held that a physical screen designed to prevent the witness from seeing the defendant is an “obvious” confrontation violation absent the narrow exception recognized in Maryland v. Craig. Craig permits restricting face-to-face confrontation for child witnesses only upon a case-specific, evidence-based finding of necessity—i.e., after the trial court hears evidence and determines this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence—and a statute or generalized assumption cannot substitute for that individualized determination. On this record, using a screen without such findings undermines procedural fairness and risks normalizing a categorical deprivation of confrontation in child-sex-abuse cases, contrary to Coy/Craig’s constitutional prerequisites; any harmless-error analysis cannot retroactively supply the required necessity finding.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause permits a trial court to block a child witness’s face-to-face view of the defendant with a screen without making case-specific, on-the-record findings that the measure is necessary to prevent trauma to that particular child.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause), as applied to a Mississippi procedure/statute described as mandatory (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) is referenced in the excerpts) requiring use of a screen for certain child witnesses.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Pitts argues the Mississippi courts upheld a confrontation-limiting screen procedure based on a generalized, legislatively presumed risk of trauma rather than the individualized necessity findings required by Supreme Court precedent. He contends the trial judge treated the screen as mandatory, expressed constitutional concern, and made no case-specific determination that this child would be traumatized by seeing him. Because the screen functioned like the face-to-face denial condemned in Coy, and because Craig allows deviations only upon a particularized necessity finding, the decision is directly contrary to controlling precedent; Pitts also urges that the error is structural or at least not harmless under the proper confrontation analysis and warrants summary reversal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Mississippi argues confrontation’s essential purposes were satisfied because the child testified under oath, was subject to cross-examination, and was observed by the jury, and the trial court determined a protective screen was necessary to prevent trauma. The State also emphasizes that any error was harmless in light of overwhelming independent evidence of guilt, including testimony from other witnesses, the child’s statements to authorities, and the videotaped forensic interview (which it notes was admissible under Mississippi tender-years rules and was introduced at trial).

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is the functional-safeguards/harmless-error argument: oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation were preserved, so any missing finding should be treated as a technicality. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Craig makes a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding the constitutional predicate for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation; harmless-error analysis cannot supply that missing authorization after the fact without converting Craig’s narrow exception into something close to a presumption. Coy reinforces that we cannot rest on generalized legislative assumptions or an effectively mandatory statutory procedure in lieu of an individualized judicial determination. The narrow, institutionally legitimate course is to reverse for lack of the Craig findings and remand, leaving any harmlessness question—if it is available at all—to the lower court under the proper standard.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point—oath, cross-examination, and jury observation preserved confrontation’s functional safeguards and any missing Craig finding is harmless—fails because the Sixth Amendment’s text (“to be confronted”) and its original public meaning require face-to-face confrontation absent a properly established exception. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Maryland v. Craig conditions any departure on a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding, and Coy rejects substituting generalized legislative judgments or routine practice for that individualized judicial predicate. Harmless-error review presupposes a constitutionally valid basis to depart from the face-to-face baseline; it cannot retroactively supply the missing authorization to deny confrontation in the first place. With no such finding here, the constitutional violation is complete and reversal is required.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s strongest point is the one I previously found attractive: because the child testified under oath, was cross-examined, and the jury could observe demeanor, the omission of explicit Craig findings should be treated as harmless. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that, under Maryland v. Craig as written and Coy’s warning against categorical substitutes, those reliability indicia are necessary but not sufficient; the case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding is the constitutional predicate for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation in the first place. Justice Gorsuch’s point further persuades me that appellate harmless-error review cannot supply that missing authorization after the fact without turning Craig’s narrow exception into a routine, statute-driven departure. Given the record’s failure to show the required particularized determination (that the defendant’s presence would so traumatize this child as to impair communication), reversal and remand is the restrained, precedent-faithful course.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is Alito’s practical/harmless-error argument: oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation were preserved and remands are costly, especially in child-victim cases. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Maryland v. Craig treats those reliability features as necessary but not sufficient; the constitutional predicate is a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding that this particular child could not reasonably communicate in the defendant’s presence, and Coy forbids substituting generalized statutory assumptions for that individualized inquiry. Justice Gorsuch’s point reinforces why appellate harmless-error review cannot supply the missing authorization after the fact—doing so would normalize a shortcut and convert Craig’s narrow exception into a routine practice, with real-world fairness consequences for defendants and vulnerable witnesses alike. The sound, administrable, precedent-faithful course is reversal and remand so the lower court applies Craig properly before any harmlessness assessment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed by Justice Alito earlier—was that the core confrontation “reliability” features (oath, cross, demeanor observation) were present and any gap in explicit Craig findings should be treated as harmless. But as the Chief Justice stresses, Craig makes those features necessary, not sufficient; the constitutionally required predicate is a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding that this child could not reasonably communicate in the defendant’s presence, and Coy forbids letting a generally applicable statute or routine practice stand in for that individualized determination. Pragmatically, requiring that narrow front-end finding is what keeps Craig administrable and cabined, and appellate harmless-error review cannot supply the missing authorization after the fact without turning a limited exception into an effectively automatic screen regime. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers framing reinforces the same point: once we allow legislatures (or appellate courts) to “backfill” necessity, we effectively rewrite Craig’s condition rather than applying it.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that the traditional confrontation values—oath, cross-examination, and demeanor evidence—were satisfied and that any deficiency in explicit findings should be treated as harmless. But Maryland v. Craig did not make face-to-face confrontation optional whenever reliability indicia are present; it conditioned the exception on a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding after hearing evidence that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence, and Coy v. Iowa rejects generalized legislative assumptions as a substitute. Even if the trial judge reviewed materials, that is not the constitutionally required predicate determination; allowing Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) to operate effectively as mandatory would let legislatures dilute a Sixth Amendment guarantee contrary to separation-of-powers principles and controlling precedent, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasized. Harmless-error arguments cannot supply the missing Craig finding; at most they address remedy after we identify the constitutional violation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Respondent’s strongest point (as Justice Alito previously framed it) is that the oath, cross-examination, and jury observation of demeanor were preserved, so a remand for more explicit findings risks elevating form over substance. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Maryland v. Craig treats those reliability features as necessary—not sufficient—and makes a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding the constitutional predicate for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation; without that predicate, we drift toward the generalized approach Coy forbids. Allowing appellate courts to infer necessity from the cold record would effectively convert Craig’s narrow exception into a routine practice, undermining administrability and the Court’s legitimacy by diluting a core Sixth Amendment protection through after-the-fact speculation. The institutionally modest course is to enforce Craig’s prerequisite by reversing and remanding, without expanding the confrontation exception beyond what precedent permits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation preserved confrontation’s functional safeguards and any missing explicit Craig finding can be treated as harmless—fails because Maryland v. Craig makes the case-specific, on-the-record necessity determination the constitutional predicate for dispensing with the Sixth Amendment’s face-to-face baseline. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, permitting appellate courts to infer necessity from a cold record would convert Craig’s narrow exception into a largely automatic statutory regime, precisely what Coy forbids when it rejects generalized assumptions standing in for individualized judicial findings. Textually and in original public meaning, the right “to be confronted” is not satisfied by reliability proxies alone absent the properly found necessity that authorizes departure in the first place. The restrained, precedent-faithful remedy is reversal for lack of Craig findings, with any harmlessness inquiry addressed, if at all, only after the correct constitutional standard is applied on remand.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—pressed through Justice Alito’s earlier “substantial compliance/harmless error” framing—is that oath, cross-examination, and demeanor observation preserved reliability, making any omission in findings effectively harmless. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Craig makes reliability indicia necessary, not sufficient; the constitutional permission to deny face-to-face confrontation turns on a case-specific, on-the-record necessity finding, and Coy forbids replacing that individualized determination with a de facto categorical screen practice. From a procedural-fairness and practical-consequences perspective, letting appellate courts infer necessity after the fact would erode the administrable front-end safeguard that keeps the Craig exception narrow and prevents routinized deprivation of confrontation. Harmless-error review may speak to remedy after a violation is identified, but it cannot supply the missing authorization to dispense with confrontation in the first place.

John Roberts.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa held that using a screen to prevent a witness from seeing the defendant is a serious infringement of the Sixth Amendment’s face-to-face confrontation right and cannot rest on generalized legislative assumptions. Maryland v. Craig permits a departure from face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding of necessity that the particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence; treating Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) as effectively mandatory without such individualized findings is contrary to Craig’s requirement. While cross-examination, oath, and jury observation satisfy important confrontation values, Craig makes clear they do not alone justify dispensing with face-to-face confrontation absent the requisite necessity determination. Given the institutional importance of adherence to controlling precedent and the narrow ground available, I would reverse for failure to make the Craig findings, leaving any harmless-error assessment to the lower courts on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause guarantees the accused a right to face-to-face confrontation, and a screen that blocks the witness’s view of the defendant is a direct infringement of that textual protection. Under Coy v. Iowa, such a screen is an “obvious” violation absent an adequate justification, and Maryland v. Craig permits departures from face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding that the measure is necessary to protect the particular child witness from trauma. A mandatory or legislatively presumed rule under Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) cannot substitute for the individualized necessity determination Craig requires, so using the screen without such findings contravenes the Sixth Amendment’s original meaning and controlling precedent. Because the constitutional defect goes to the manner of testimony itself—denial of face-to-face confrontation—this Court should not uphold the conviction on the basis of generalized assumptions rather than constitutionally required findings.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s core protections—oath, cross-examination, and observation of demeanor by the trier of fact—were satisfied here, even if the child did not have an unobstructed face-to-face view of the defendant. Maryland v. Craig allows dispensing with literal face-to-face confrontation when necessary to protect a child witness and when reliability is otherwise assured; on this record, the trial court heard evidence, reviewed the forensic interview, and inquired into the need for a screen, which is sufficient to avoid turning Craig into a rigid formula. Even assuming the court’s findings were not as explicit as Craig prefers, the practical consequences and the State’s strong independent evidence of guilt support affirmance under harmless-error principles rather than reversal for a procedural shortcoming. Coy v. Iowa is distinguishable because it involved a categorical screen imposed without the kind of necessity inquiry Craig contemplates.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa treats a screen that blocks a child witness’s view of the defendant as a direct, serious denial of face-to-face confrontation, and Maryland v. Craig permits such a deviation only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding that the measure is necessary to protect the welfare of the particular child witness. A procedure applied as mandatory under Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g), without individualized necessity findings tied to this child (not a generalized legislative presumption of trauma), is contrary to Craig’s requirement that the trial court “hear evidence” and determine necessity in the specific case. Requiring those findings both safeguards defendants’ Sixth Amendment rights and ensures any protective measures are narrowly tailored to the child’s actual needs, rather than imposed automatically. Because the trial court here lacked the constitutionally required individualized findings, I would vote to reverse and remand for proceedings consistent with Craig.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa treats face-to-face confrontation as the Sixth Amendment baseline, and Maryland v. Craig permits departure only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence such that the child could not reasonably communicate. A mandatory or effectively automatic screen procedure under Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g), applied without individualized necessity findings, is inconsistent with Craig’s constitutional condition for dispensing with face-to-face confrontation, even if other confrontation features (oath, cross-examination, jury observation) were present. Because the error here goes to the constitutional prerequisite for denying face-to-face confrontation, the State’s generalized legislative presumption of trauma cannot substitute for the trial judge’s individualized determination required by Craig and reinforced by Coy’s insistence on a particularized showing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the accused a face-to-face confrontation, and Coy v. Iowa condemns the use of a screen that blocks a child witness’s view of the defendant absent an adequate justification. Maryland v. Craig permits a departure from face-to-face confrontation only upon a “case-specific” finding of necessity made on the record after hearing evidence that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence. A mandatory, statute-driven practice (Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g) as applied) that dispenses with individualized findings cannot be squared with Craig’s requirement and risks allowing the legislature to dictate courtroom procedure in derogation of a constitutional guarantee. Whatever the strength of the State’s harmless-error claim, the threshold constitutional rule is that courts may not deny face-to-face confrontation without the particularized findings Craig demands.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Coy v. Iowa recognizes the Sixth Amendment’s strong preference for face-to-face confrontation and rejects blanket, generalized assumptions as a substitute for necessity. Maryland v. Craig permits an exception only upon a case-specific, on-the-record finding that denying face-to-face confrontation is necessary to further an important public policy—i.e., that this particular child would be traumatized by the defendant’s presence—and only if the procedure otherwise preserves the essence of confrontation through oath, cross-examination, and observation. A mandatory screen procedure under Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g), applied without individualized findings, is difficult to reconcile with Craig’s requirement of a “proper finding of necessity” and risks becoming the kind of categorical rule Coy disapproved. Given the Court’s duty to apply controlling precedent and insist on workable, administrable safeguards, I would vote to reverse and require individualized findings before the screen may be used.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause’s text guarantees the accused the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” and this Court has treated face-to-face confrontation as the baseline requirement. In Coy v. Iowa, we held that a screen preventing the child witnesses from seeing the defendant was an “obvious” violation absent an individualized showing, rejecting reliance on generalized legislative judgments. Maryland v. Craig recognized only a narrow exception, and it conditioned any denial of face-to-face confrontation on case-specific, on-the-record findings—after hearing evidence—that the measure is necessary to protect that particular child from trauma. Because Mississippi’s procedure was treated as mandatory and applied without individualized necessity findings for this child, it is contrary to Craig and Coy; any harmless-error argument cannot supply the constitutionally required predicate finding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause presumptively guarantees face-to-face confrontation, and Coy v. Iowa makes clear that a screen blocking the witness’s view of the accused is a denial of that right absent an adequate, case-specific justification. Maryland v. Craig permits such a deviation only upon individualized, on-the-record findings that denial of face-to-face confrontation is necessary to further an important public policy (protecting a particular child witness) and that the reliability of testimony is otherwise assured; a mandatory or legislatively presumed trauma rule cannot substitute for the trial judge’s particularized necessity determination. Here, the Mississippi procedure (as applied under Miss. Code Ann. § 99-43-101(2)(g)) was treated as effectively mandatory without case-specific findings that this child would be traumatized by seeing the defendant, which is contrary to Craig’s procedural-fairness requirements. Given the centrality of confrontation to adversarial testing, I would not uphold a regime that dispenses with individualized findings and instead relies on generalized assumptions about trauma.
